svg.aria-label: Diagram: what a Kinesis partition key does, and what Service-Managed Partition Keys changes. On the left, the existing behaviour: a producer must specify a partition key with every record, an MD5 hash function maps that key to a 128-bit integer, and the record lands in whichever shard owns that hash key range. This single mechanism delivers two separate properties at once. The first is distribution, spreading records across shards, which fails when one key value carries a disproportionate share of traffic and saturates its shard while the others sit idle. The second is ordering, because each record's sequence number is unique per partition key within its shard and sequence numbers for the same partition key generally increase over time, so all records sharing a key arrive in order on one shard. In the centre, the shard limits that are unchanged by this launch: 1,000 records per second and 1 megabyte per second for writes, 2 megabytes per second and 5 transactions per second for reads, with partition keys themselves counting toward the write byte limit, and the two write ceilings meeting at about 1 kilobyte per record. On the right, the new behaviour: the producer specifies no partition key, and the service distributes records based on available warm capacity, which removes the hot-shard failure entirely. A closing panel records the trade, that distribution and ordering were always the same mechanism, so opting out of the hot shard also opts out of the per-key ordering guarantee, which is why the announcement scopes the feature to workloads where record ordering is not required. It applies to On-Demand Standard and On-Demand Advantage streams, in all commercial regions, at no additional cost, adopted by upgrading the SDK or Kinesis Producer Library.
svg.title: One mechanism, two guarantees — and you cannot give up only one
svg.text: The partition key spreads the load and orders the records. It is one mechanism.
So the feature that removes the hot shard also removes the ordering guarantee. That is the whole trade.
Today — the producer must specify a key
partition key → MD5 → 128-bit integer → shard hash range
Job 1 — distribution
Spreads records across shards. Indifferent to how much
traffic any one key value carries — this is the hot shard.
Job 2 — ordering
Sequence numbers are unique per partition key within a
shard. Same key → same shard → in order.
Service-Managed Partition Keys
no key supplied → service places the record
Job 1 — solved properly
Distributes “based on available warm capacity” — an
input a hash function never had. No hot shard.
Job 2 — given up with it
No key means no per-key co-location, so no per-key
order. Scoped to “where record ordering is not required”.
Unchanged by this launch — the shard is still the unit of capacity
writes: 1,000 records/sec and 1 MB/sec — and the partition keys themselves count toward that byte limit
reads: 2 MB/sec and 5 transactions/sec · the two write ceilings meet at about 1 KB per record
Why you cannot have both
Order is not a separate feature. Records stay in order because they share a key, and sharing a key is what
puts them on one shard — which is also exactly what makes that shard hot. Same property, read two ways.
The check belongs downstream: not “does the producer need order”, but “does any consumer assume it”.
On-Demand Standard and On-Demand Advantage · all commercial Regions · no additional cost · upgrade the SDK or KPL.
It is set per record, so one stream can carry ordered entities and unordered telemetry side by side.
